title: Forecasting Research Trends
answer: Forecasting research trends uses citation mapping and discovery to identify emerging topics, influential papers, and shifting research fronts before they become established. It draws on bibliometric signals such as co-citation clusters, reference age, and author networks, and it treats the research literature as a structured graph rather than a simple list of publications. The site's library of 135 research papers, 10,555 extracted claims, and 801 scientific models provides a working corpus for this kind of analysis. The aim is to give researchers and research managers an early view of where a field is heading, not to predict individual breakthroughs.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Forecasting research trends uses citation mapping and discovery to identify emerging topics, influential papers, and shifting research fronts before they become established. It draws on bibliometric signals such as co-citation clusters, reference age, and author networks, and it treats the research literature as a structured graph rather than a simple list of publications. The site's library of 135 research papers, 10,555 extracted claims, and 801 scientific models provides a working corpus for this kind of analysis. The aim is to give researchers and research managers an early view of where a field is heading, not to predict individual breakthroughs.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a combination of citation indexes, full-text repositories, and graph databases that store paper-to-paper and paper-to-claim relationships. Processing is typically done with Python or R pipelines that pull metadata, parse reference lists, and build co-citation or bibliographic coupling matrices. The site's catalogue of 91 AI books, 732 AI tools, and 674 glossary terms sits alongside the paper library as a reference layer, but the core computation is over citation edges and extracted claims. No special hardware is required for most trend forecasting tasks; standard cloud compute or a single workstation is enough for tens of thousands of papers.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual approach is to construct a citation graph, cluster papers by shared references or shared citing behaviour, and then track how clusters grow, merge, or fade over time. Researchers also extract claims from papers, here 10,555 claims are available, and watch for claims that begin to be cited across disciplinary boundaries. Trend scores often combine citation velocity, author mobility, and the novelty of term combinations in titles and abstracts. The output is a ranked set of emerging topics or research fronts, each tied back to the original papers rather than to a secondary search tool.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Citation-based forecasting carries clear risks of reinforcing existing prestige hierarchies, because highly cited work from well known groups is easier to see than quiet but important work from smaller labs. There is also a provenance obligation to link every trend claim to the underlying paper, and this site does that by linking to the original publication rather than to an aggregator. Rights issues are mostly about access to full-text and metadata, which varies by publisher, and about not treating a trend score as a judgement of individual researchers. The extracted claims need versioning and source tracking so that a forecast can be audited back to the sentence or figure that supported it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward combining citation graphs with full-text language models so that trends can be detected from the content of claims, not only from who cites whom. Research trend forecasting is also likely to become more continuous, with weekly or daily updates instead of annual reviews, as preprint servers and open citation data grow. The site's structured library of papers, claims, models, tools, and glossary terms points toward a more integrated research atlas where a trend is shown with its key papers, methods, and terminology in one place. The main open problem is distinguishing a real shift from a short-lived spike in attention.
